topics.title: Share Hero and Snowball checkpoint export mechanics
topics.body:
Share HF shard writing between Hero and the Levanter converter used by Snowball. A private writer owns host memory reservations, uploads and optional resume receipts. Callers keep model conversion, shard layout and destination policy.

Call from all JAX ranks with identical shard/key order and matching shapes/dtypes. Only process zero writes. Resume verifies identity and checksums before reuse. Writer failures propagate when a main thread observes them.

CPU tests cover exact output parity, BF16 shapes, budget limits, two-rank failure/recovery and Snowball overwrites. Formatting and types pass. Full-size accelerator and live cloud/HF uploads remain untested.

topics.title: [iris] Quarantine nodes with persistent isolated S3 failures
topics.body:
Add opt-in regional S3 read/write/delete probes to the Kubernetes node-agent so a node that remains Ready while storage requests stall can be quarantined before it receives more work. The probe uses the task storage environment, a tiny object per node incarnation, and a process deadline that bounds SDK retries and DNS stalls.

The controller cordons persistent failures only when a fresh majority of nodes successfully probed the same target after the failure began. A persistent cordon budget defaults to one node, and credential/configuration errors reset the failure streak. Node UID, boot ID, report freshness, and Kubernetes resource versions fence stale observations and concurrent operator changes.

Health and cordon evidence remain in node annotations even when Finelog is unavailable. Recovery requires an operator to uncordon the repaired node and release its budget annotation; running tasks are not evicted. Configuration, scratch-object lifecycle requirements, and recovery are documented in the CoreWeave guide.

Context: [node-local storage failure during the hero run](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/599).

topics.title: Pod creation fails on a node with 65K empty Silo cgroups
topics.body:
On October 2, new pods failed to start on CoreWeave node `g5bc6da`, blocking new jobs. Kubernetes reported `no space left on device` while creating a pod’s cgroup, the kernel group used to track and limit container resources. The node still reported healthy, and its filesystem had 3.55 TB free.

The host cgroup tree had 65,535 descendant groups. Of these, 65,412 were under `/silo`; that entire subtree contained no processes. This strongly suggests exhaustion of the kernel’s roughly 64K memory-cgroup ID space, though we have not traced the failing allocator.

Silo is the nested container runtime running inside our privileged Iris job `muchanem.cap-pipeline-host-53`. Two sampled container IDs from its `containerd-shim` processes matched empty `/silo` cgroups. This points to a cleanup problem in that workload’s runtime, but we have not identified the code path responsible. We have no evidence that CoreWeave’s host containerd created these groups.

Please investigate whether completed containers leave cgroups and shim processes behind, and fix the cleanup path. Verify that repeated container creation and teardown do not keep increasing either count. Coordinate cleanup of the affected node with the pipeline owner; an empty cgroup alone does not establish that it is safe to remove while the runtime is active.

---

topics.title: [iris] Seven cordoned H100 nodes in cw-us-east-02a cannot start their reboot
topics.body:
Seven of the 32 H100 nodes in `cw-us-east-02a` are cordoned and wait for a CoreWeave production reboot. The reboot cannot start, because Iris task pods are still on each node. Some of these nodes have been out of service since 2026-09-30, so about 22% of the cluster's H100 capacity is unavailable. GPU gang jobs that need this capacity stay pending.

CoreWeave's node lifecycle controller (NLCC) cordoned each node after the kernel watchdog reported a CPU soft lockup (`KernelDeadlock`). It then moved the node to the `production-reboot` pending state (`NLCCPendingExitProduction`). The reboot happens after the workload pods leave. The HPC verification passes on all seven nodes.

| ga8db08 | 2026-10-01 20:30 | soft lockup | triage (DCGM diagnostic timed out on 2026-10-03 13:05) | 59,724 | 1 (`cap-construct-003-shard-012-v2`) |
| g845f9c | 2026-10-01 21:08 | `AwsEventLoop` | production-reboot | 59,460 | 1 (`cap-construct-003-shard-005-v2`) |
| g83d11c | 2026-10-01 23:31 | `VLLM::EngineCor` | production-reboot | 59,342 | 4 (`cap-pipeline-broker-v4`, `glm53-autoscaler`, `glm53-relay-telemetry`, `glm53-telemetry-2`) |

| g73e352 | 2026-10-02 06:40 | `AwsEventLoop` | production-reboot | 59,695 | 1 (`cap-pipeline-host-51`) |
| g83d3ee | 2026-10-02 06:54 | `AwsEventLoop` | production-reboot | 30,561 | 2 (`cap-construct-003-shard-060-v2`, `glm53-relay-e`) |

Observations:

- Five nodes still report `KernelDeadlock=True`, with later soft lockups on 2026-10-02 and 2026-10-03. Several of those are in the kernel's own `migration/N` threads.
- All seven nodes ran Silo host pods, and six still hold tens of thousands of leaked `/silo` cgroups (#9696). The memory-cgroup limit is 65,535. A link between the leak and the soft lockups is not established.

- The Iris task pods leave the seven nodes, through Iris preemption or a stop of each job, without Silo host pods moving to other nodes.
- NLCC completes the reboot of each node, and CoreWeave completes the triage of `ga8db08`. Each node is back in `production`, uncordoned, with `KernelDeadlock=False` and fewer than 2,000 memory cgroups.
- A new pod starts on each node.

3. For other Iris tasks, delete the pod with the default grace period. Iris starts a new attempt on another node. `iris task preempt` from the `marin` hub did not take effect for these federated tasks, and `kubectl drain` is blocked by the per-attempt PodDisruptionBudgets.

Seven Silo host jobs were stopped in the process (`cap-pipeline-host-25`, `-26`, `-29`, `-40`, `-41`, `-44`, `-51`). 18 still run. The underlying leak is tracked in #9696.

Closing, since all cordoned nodes are back in service or replaced.

## Overview

This living policy defines which evaluation results for Marin models and comparison baselines are reportable, public-facing, and canonical. It records the evaluations, their hyperparameters and experimental constraints, and the self-contained codebase needed to reproduce the results independently. The policy is intended to be a trustworthy snapshot for each period in which it applies.

The first Snowball 67B A2B MoE release brings regular comparisons with existing open and closed-source models. Marin's open-development claim requires transparent reporting of evaluation scores and the capability claims based on them.

## Previous version notes

* Released Sept 24, 2026: 18 non-agentic benchmarks, 8 Harbor agentic benchmarks, and 4 reserved out-of-distribution benchmarks.

## Complete eval list, with hyperparameters

### In Distribution

`finished_at`; for policy-valid partial seals, the final `updated_at` at sealing is used instead.
Scheduler wait and model-server startup are excluded. The table should be refreshed when the
remaining NUPA, SWE-bench Verified, and τ³ cells seal.

### Out of Distribution

* AAII 4.3
* Terminal-Bench Science
* DeepSWE 1.1 (deep-swe-litecontainer@1.1)

### Details on our Evals

- **MATH-500.** OpenAI's [May 2023 process-supervision release](https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision/) used a 500-problem subset of the original MATH competition-math benchmark. The campaign scores one zero-shot generated solution per problem by final-answer accuracy.
- **HumanEval+.** The [May 2023 EvalPlus paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210) introduced expanded tests for HumanEval programs to catch incorrect code that passes sparse original tests. The campaign executes one zero-shot completion per problem against the stronger tests.
- **MBPP+.** The [November 24, 2023 EvalPlus release](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus/releases/tag/v0.2.0) extends MBPP with additional functional tests. The campaign's pinned config is zero-shot and scores one generated program per problem.
- **OlympiadBench.** The [February 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14008) introduced bilingual, multimodal Olympiad-level math and science problems. This campaign uses Evalchemy's 30-question text subset, ten sampled solutions per question, and the configured answer judge.
- **GSM8K.** The [October 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) introduced grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic. The campaign uses the zero-shot `gsm8k-0shot` completion route and scores the extracted final answer.
- **PIQA.** The [November 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11641) introduced two-choice questions about physical commonsense. The campaign selects the answer by length-normalized log-likelihood with no examples in the prompt.
- **WinoGrande.** The [July 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10641) introduced adversarial pronoun/coreference choices designed to reduce superficial cues. The campaign uses five-shot multiple-choice scoring.
- **BoolQ.** The [May 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10044) introduced naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with evidence passages. The campaign scores zero-shot choice accuracy.
- **TruthfulQA MC2.** The [September 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07958) introduced questions that elicit common misconceptions from language models. The campaign's MC2 metric sums probability mass on all true answers within each question's candidate set, rather than counting a single selected answer.
- **TriviaQA.** The [May 2017 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03551) introduced trivia questions with independently collected evidence documents. The campaign runs five-shot answer generation and reports answer accuracy.
- **AIME24.** The [Mathematical Association of America's 2024 AIME](https://maa.org/maa-invitational-competitions/) supplies the contest problems. Evalchemy samples ten solutions per question in one run through the shared seeded-repeat implementation and scores the integer final answers.
- **MMLU-Pro.** The [June 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574) introduced harder, more reasoning-focused multiple-choice questions across fourteen subjects. The campaign runs zero-shot generation with a 65,536-token cap and reports micro-averaged accuracy.
- **GPQA Diamond.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) introduced expert-written graduate-level science questions, including the Diamond subset. The campaign averages accuracy over three generated answers per question.
- **CRUXEval (output).** The [January 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03065) introduced input- and output-prediction tasks for short Python programs. The tracker reports the output-prediction direction, scored on one generated answer per item.
- **FinanceBench.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11944) introduced questions grounded in public financial filings. The campaign scores one generated answer per question with its pinned LLM judge.
- **IFBench.** The [July 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02833) introduced verifiable constraints that test generalization in precise instruction following. The campaign reports strict prompt-level accuracy, requiring every constraint to hold in the raw response.
- **MRCR.** [Gemini's September 2024 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) introduced multi-round coreference resolution; [OpenAI's public MRCR release (April 2025)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr) supplies the corrected multi-needle data used here. The campaign scores nonce-gated sequence similarity and selects only context-length bins that fit the served model.
- **NUPA stratified (Loose).** The [November 2024 Number Cookbook paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03766) introduced tests of numerical understanding and processing across representations and tasks. The campaign uses Evalchemy's pinned `NUPA5K-Loose` benchmark: a deterministic 5,000-record stratified sample covering 44 tasks and 2,391 strata, scored with permissive answer extraction rather than the paper's direct-answer protocol. Its longest rendered prompt is 399 tokens under Evalchemy's reference tokenizer; the standard 256-token prompt cushion and 64-token endpoint guard leave a 72,945-token response cap inside the 73,664-token single-turn context window.
- **SWE-bench Verified.** OpenAI's [August 13, 2024 release](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) introduced the 500-task, human-validated repository-issue repair set. The campaign runs Harbor's canonical `swebench-verified@1.0` implementation with mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, one trial per issue, and executable verification.
- **OpenThoughts-TBLite 2.0.** The [February 18, 2026 release](https://www.openthoughts.ai/blog/openthoughts-tblite) introduced a 100-task, faster-running terminal-agent panel calibrated against Terminal-Bench 2. The campaign runs its pinned `openthoughts-tblite@2.0` tasks with Terminus-2, three trials per task, and reports mean verifier success across trials.
- **Terminal-Bench 2.1.** The [November 7, 2025 release](https://www.tbench.ai/news/announcement-2-0) introduced a harder, more thoroughly verified terminal-agent task set alongside Harbor. The campaign uses `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1` at ref 6 through Harbor, with three Terminus-2 trials per task, a 65,536-token context window, and a 16,384-token per-turn output cap.
- **DS-1000 mini-200.** The [November 2022 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11501) introduced data-science code-generation problems spanning seven Python libraries. The campaign evaluates a fixed seed-42 200-task Harbor subset with Terminus-2, building task images from the pinned Dockerfiles.
- **BFCL-Parity @ Pi.** Berkeley's [February 2024 BFCL release](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html) introduced executable function-calling evaluation. This campaign uses the Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent, so its score is the pinned adaptation's verified solve rate rather than an unqualified BFCL leaderboard score.
- **BixBench CLI corrections @ Pi.** The [February 2025 BixBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096) introduced multi-step computational-biology analysis tasks. This campaign uses Pi on 205 `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` tasks and reports binary answer-equivalence reward, which is distinct from canonical BixBench CLI v1.5.
- **τ³-bench @ Pi.** Sierra's [March 18, 2026 τ³-Bench launch](https://sierra.ai/blog/bench-advancing-agent-benchmarking-to-knowledge-and-voice) introduced knowledge and voice tracks alongside corrections to the existing airline and retail tasks. The campaign runs pinned `tau3-bench@1.0.1` in Harbor through the Pi ACP relay and scores task verification.
- **SOTOPIA-hard.** The [October 2023 SOTOPIA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11667) introduced interactive social-agent evaluation and identified a hard scenario subset. The campaign runs the 100 hard episodes against a fixed `openai/gpt-oss-120b` counterpart and judge, then normalizes goal achievement from 0–10 to 0–1.

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We may** -- evaluate our final models on out-of-distribution benchmarks

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited)

### Metric definitions

- **`accuracy`:** the fraction of scored items that pass the benchmark's configured correctness check. The common name covers executable-test success for code and agent tasks, answer correctness for generated and multiple-choice tasks, FinanceBench's `correct` judge label, and BixBench's binary answer-equivalence check. NUPA Loose applies format-specific, permissive answer extraction before a representation-sensitive exact match. PIQA chooses the option with the highest length-normalized log-likelihood before testing correctness. AIME24 and OlympiadBench average ten seeded samples per item; GPQA Diamond averages three. MMLU-Pro is micro-averaged across its fourteen subjects.
- **`mc2`:** TruthfulQA's probability mass on all true answers, normalized over the question's answer set and averaged over questions. It is not a binary selection accuracy, and chance performance is above zero.
- **`accuracy (output)`:** CRUXEval output-prediction accuracy. Given a function and input, the model predicts the output; this is distinct from CRUXEval input prediction, which reconstructs an input from the function and desired output.
- **`strict prompt-level accuracy`:** the fraction of IFBench prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **`mean sequence similarity`:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit. The standard 73,728-token serving window evaluates the published bins through 65,536 tokens. After Marin's 64-token serving safety margin, the 32,768-token models use bins through 16,384 and the 65,536-token model uses bins through 32,768. Those tracker cells are footnoted because differing bin coverage is not a strictly like-for-like comparison.
- **`normalized goal achievement`:** SOTOPIA-hard's official goal-achievement score for the evaluated character, linearly normalized from `[0, 10]` to `[0, 1]` and averaged over the 100 official hard episodes. The counterpart and evaluator are fixed to `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together for every model.

### Other Metric Notes

- **Scale:** every metric in the suite is reported on a 0-1 scale with 1 the best and 0 the worst; there are no error counts, ranks, or unbounded scores.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. For standard multi-turn benchmarks, max generation length per turn is capped at 8192. Context-ablation labels are `context window / per-turn output limit`: both values are passed explicitly, with the first applied to vLLM `max_model_len` and Pi `model_info.max_input_tokens`, and the second applied to Pi `model_info.max_output_tokens`. For example, `65k-16k` means a 65,536-token serving and Pi context window with a 16,384-token per-turn output limit.
- **Pi runtime:** Agentic Pi configs must pin `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` explicitly. The corrected context control pins Pi `0.87.0`; the original harness result used unpinned Pi `0.86.1`, while the first context-ablation rerun drifted to unpinned Pi `0.87.0`. Results from different Pi versions are not treated as a controlled context-only comparison.

### LLM judges

Five evals involve an LLM judge; every other eval in the suite grades programmatically
(IFBench verifies each constraint with its checker functions, MRCR uses `SequenceMatcher`,
the math evals use Minerva/SymPy, the multiple-choice evals compare selections, and the
remaining harness/agentic evals run test suites).

- **FinanceBench:** every scored response is judged. The judge sees the question, the
  reference answers, and the candidate, and returns one label: `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` (equivalent answers in substance count as correct — algebraic equivalence,
  unit conversions, rounding). Only `correct` scores.
- **BixBench CLI correction set:** every submitted answer is judged for semantic equivalence
  to the task's ideal answer and receives a binary reward. A missing answer receives zero
  without invoking the judge.
- **OlympiadBench:** Minerva/SymPy grades first, and the judge answers equivalence only for
  answers Minerva cannot establish; the reported scores come from the offline regrade, which
  uses this judge the same way (see "OlympiadBench regrade" below).
- **SOTOPIA-hard:** the official episode evaluator judges goal achievement for the evaluated
  character after each completed social interaction and returns the 0–10 score that the metric
  normalizes to 0–1.
- **τ³-bench:** the verifier combines deterministic task checks with an LLM evaluator for
  natural-language assertions. The separately configured LLM that simulates the user is part of
  the task environment, not the judge.

Judge deployment is benchmark-specific:

- **FinanceBench and OlympiadBench** use `openai/gpt-oss-120b` through Together. The launch
  configuration supplies `JUDGE_MODEL`, `JUDGE_BASE_URL`, and a Together API key.
- **BixBench** uses a co-hosted `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8` judge at revision
  `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`. Marin serves it on eight H100s with tensor
  parallelism 8, a 32,768-token context window, the `minimax_m3` reasoning parser, prefix
  caching, and CUDA graphs enabled. The verifier receives the co-hosted endpoint and model
  identity directly from Marin; it does not use the Together judge environment.
- **SOTOPIA-hard** uses `openai/gpt-oss-120b` through Together for both the fixed counterpart
  and the official episode evaluator. Its LiteLLM identifier is
  `openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b`: the first segment selects the OpenAI-compatible provider and
  the remainder is Together's model ID.
- **τ³-bench** uses that same Together-hosted model and LiteLLM identifier for both the user
  simulator and the natural-language assertion evaluator. The two roles are independently
  configured even though this campaign pins them to the same checkpoint.

Judge hyperparameters, per path:

- **Answer-equivalence judge** (FinanceBench, OlympiadBench): a single user message with the
  three-way rubric, `temperature=0`, request timeout 300 s with 5 transport retries, and 16
  concurrent judgments per run. `max_tokens` starts at 128 and escalates 128 → 512 → 2048
  when a completion comes back empty — a hosted reasoning model can spend a small completion
  budget on hidden reasoning and return no content — so the ladder guarantees the final label
  lands within budget. The context window is gpt-oss-120b's 131,072 tokens as served
  (Together); no truncation of the graded material happens judge-side. The raw completion is
  retained in the results for audit, alongside the parsed label.
- **BixBench verifier:** the verifier calls the co-hosted MiniMax Chat Completions endpoint
  with `max_tokens=1024` and a structured response schema containing one boolean score.
  Sampling follows the endpoint's service defaults.
- **SOTOPIA evaluator:** the pinned SOTOPIA v0.1.5 evaluator uses the fixed judge model after
  each episode; the model under evaluation never acts as its own judge.
- **τ³ natural-language assertions:** the pinned τ³ adapter passes only assertions that need
  semantic evaluation to its configured LLM; deterministic assertions remain programmatic.

When a judge call fails after retries, the sample is recorded as grader infrastructure
failure (counted against the run's error tolerance) rather than silently scored zero.

### Thinking mode

The main table records the policy for every benchmark. `on` and `off` set
`enable_thinking` through the model or benchmark config; a benchmark override wins over the model
default. `model default` means the benchmark adds no override, and `not applicable` means the task
does not use a generated chat response. If a model cannot turn reasoning off (e.g. GPT-OSS), an `off` benchmark
uses the model's lowest available reasoning setting instead.

### Errors and Exceptions

#### Infrastructure Error Tolerance

An evaluation may be sealed as soon as at least 90% of its declared trials have valid scores under
the campaign configuration. Up to 10% of declared trials may be absent because of infrastructure
failures; the result does not need to wait for those trials to be recovered. Reported uncertainty
must include this infrastructure-failure tolerance. Task-level outcomes, including agent timeouts
recorded as scores of zero, are scored trials rather than infrastructure failures.

#### Zero-score trace audit

A score of exactly zero shall be reported only after agent review of at least ten representative
traces, or every trace when the evaluation has fewer than ten. The review will check model output,
harness parsing, verifier output, and serving or sandbox errors and accept the zero when the traces support model or task failure and no untracked infrastructure failure explains the result. Otherwise, the result should be rejected and re-run under the policy.

#### Infrastructure vs Model Error

We categorize errors during the evaluation process as either infrastructure errors or model errors.
Model errors are scoreable and do not count toward the infrastructure-error threshold. Unless this
policy explicitly identifies an error as a model error, it is an infrastructure error.

##### Harbor

For Harbor evals, the following error types are currently treated as score-able model errors.

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.

For these Harbor score-able model errors, we terminate the trial and then run the verifier on the output of the agent, if any output is present. Unlike the Evalchemy timeout rule above, we do *not* automatically score Harbor model errors as 0's. This is because sometimes, agents will solve the task correctly and then get stuck in a loop of self-doubt or fail to submit properly in their harness, and we regard that outcome as closer to a success than a failure.

##### Ambiguous Harbor Errors

- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing scoreable work. We treat these errors as score-able but if a trial returns more than 30% NonZeroAgentExitCodeError the agent or human executing the policy should review the traces to look for infrastructure errors and invalidate the run if any are discovered.

##### Evalchemy

Under the current Evalchemy pin, `malformed_model_response` is the only named error category that
remains scoreable. It means the model endpoint returned a response that Evalchemy could not parse,
or returned no usable final-answer content. Evalchemy substitutes an empty generation, preserves
the diagnostic category, and lets the benchmark grade that generation normally; this will usually,
but not necessarily, score zero.

`AgentTimeoutError`, `model_transport`, and `grader_infrastructure` are currently serialized with
the `EVALCHEMY_INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR` marker and excluded from scored coverage. They therefore count
against the 10% infrastructure-failure allowance rather than as zero-valued model outcomes. Other
task-level failures, including `generation_policy`, `generation`, `grading`, `serialization`,
`incomplete_evaluation`, and `invalid_result`, do not produce a scoreable trial.

This exposes a mismatch with the intended Evalchemy timeout rule below: the release policy says an
`AgentTimeoutError` should score `0.0`, but the current pinned implementation treats it as
infrastructure. Results and coverage from this pin must follow the recorded implementation behavior;
making Evalchemy timeouts scoreable requires a new code pin and provenance.



#### Timeout Policy

The following limits apply to every policy benchmark; there are no benchmark-specific exceptions.

| Evaluator phase | Limit | Outcome when the limit expires |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Evalchemy trial | 30 minutes | Record `0.0` as an `AgentTimeoutError`. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor agent setup | 6 minutes | Record `AgentSetupTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |
| Harbor agent execution | 30 minutes | Record `AgentTimeoutError`, preserve the agent's work, and run the verifier. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor verifier | 5 minutes | Record `VerifierTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |

The Evalchemy limit covers the full trial, including request retries and backoff, after the trial
acquires an evaluator slot.

Harbor launch configs override task-manifest values with
`agents[].override_setup_timeout_sec: 360`, `agents[].override_timeout_sec: 1800`, and
`verifier.override_timeout_sec: 300`. The repository-owned campaign validator checks these values
before submission, so the same limits apply even when a task manifest omits its own timeout.

## Baseline Models

### How we select baseline models

The process for selecting baseline models in our policy is fundamentally heuristic and community-driven. For each new model release, we will strive to select a representative cohort of open-weights and open-source models that are roughly comparable to Marin models and document them in the policy. We will look up reported results for those models in the research literature and, where available, use them as targets for internal reproduction, noting, however, that typically the variance in hyperparameters will make published results not directly comparable to our own. We will sometimes substitute quantized variants of the listed models for the canonical models, especially for larger models where our hardware makes it challenging to run inference on the non-quantized variants.

### Snowball 67B A2B Baseline Models

* Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
* Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct
* Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct
* inclusionAI/Ling-lite-1.5
* google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it
* nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-BF16
* openai/gpt-oss-20b
* nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16
* moonshotai/Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct
* arcee-ai/Trinity-Mini

## Codebase pins

| Codebase | Campaign branch | Commit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Harbor | [`benfeuer/eval-campaign-09-25`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/tree/benfeuer/eval-campaign-09-25) | [`2666d6526477ae3e46030a8dc4f3f2c68fd7a84f`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/commit/2666d6526477ae3e46030a8dc4f3f2c68fd7a84f) |
| Evalchemy | [`benfeuer/policy-context-budget`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/tree/benfeuer/policy-context-budget) | [`af61e0baaa291071f815f14f567852adece6e14c`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/af61e0baaa291071f815f14f567852adece6e14c) |
| Marin | [`benfeuer/eval-campaign-09-25-v2`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/benfeuer/eval-campaign-09-25-v2) | [`ee68254f6d16297f69a37091579ace6e2a6abae3`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/ee68254f6d16297f69a37091579ace6e2a6abae3) |

The Marin campaign launcher reads the Harbor and Evalchemy commits from Marin's checked-in external
dependency declarations and verifies that the Harbor lockfile resolves to the same commit. The
checked-out Marin commit therefore identifies all three codebase revisions. The repository-owned
campaign is

### Configuration immutability

The launcher does not alter model-serving settings or benchmark semantics. It may resolve
credentials, cluster placement, output locations, concurrency, and other operational values.
Model-specific chat templates are the sole model-config composition step: a version-controlled
template under the campaign directory is inserted into the effective model YAML. The campaign YAML
also applies its checked-in, model-specific Harbor context and compaction values. Each durable run
record preserves the effective model configuration, evaluator configuration, code revision, and
Harbor policy digest. Any other semantic change requires a new checked-in config and code revision.

SOTOPIA-hard is read from
[`open-athena/sotopia-hard-harbor`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/sotopia-hard-harbor/tree/65be6de928ab289e43a2730182b5b75cf2f75d41)

workspace.

## Run resumption

Resume an interrupted Harbor run only when its model, checked-out repository revision, runtime
limit, and dataset state are unchanged. Read the original run ID and effective configuration from
its durable `record.json`. Use the model and Harbor config from the same Marin commit, then add the
original run ID:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$CAMPAIGN/model-configs/<model-config>.yaml" \
  --harbor-config "$STAGED_HARBOR_DIR/<harbor-config>.yaml" \
  --resume-run-id <original-run-id>
```

The durable `<records-prefix>/<original-run-id>/results/harbor_jobs/` tree must remain accessible.
Harbor preserves completed scored trials and reruns missing attempts and exceptions in its pinned
resume taxonomy. Use a clean replacement when model, policy, pins, limits, records prefix, or
dataset state changed, or when the unscored error is outside that taxonomy. Never delete a trial
directory to force recovery.

## Baseline-specific launch settings

The YAML files under
`experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/model-configs/` are authoritative for checkpoint and tokenizer
revisions, serving context, GPU count, tensor and data parallelism, reasoning parser, tool parser,
sampling overrides, and Pi `thinking_format`. Use the matching file unchanged. Pi uses
`qwen-chat-template` for Qwen3.6 and Qwen3-Next and `chat-template` for the other models.

MRCR serves at 73,728 tokens and gives Evalchemy 73,664 after its 64-token safety margin. Ling
Lite's native 32,768-token window uses `mrcr-32k.yaml`; the historical 65,536-token Snowball
candidate uses `mrcr-65k.yaml`; every release-figure model uses `mrcr.yaml` otherwise. Evalchemy
evaluates only the published bins that fit.

## Updating codebase pins

Use the newest campaign pin for each codebase across the full release, assuming forward
compatibility with earlier score-producing runs. If a pin change causes an observed result
regression, stop launches, fix or revert the change, and issue a new policy version when the
evaluation behavior intentionally changes. Preserve the original run's exact pins in its immutable
config snapshot even after the release-wide pins advance.

## Standards for presenting Marin evals

* Select the release Snowball checkpoint by simple paired benchmark win rate among Snowball candidates. Release figures include only the selected checkpoint, not the other Snowball candidates. The Snowball candidate family includes the Grug 67B A2B checkpoint as well as checkpoints named Snowball. For each benchmark, plot the selected Snowball checkpoint and every non-Snowball baseline with an available score and total-training-FLOP estimate. Performance is on the y-axis and total training FLOPs are on a logarithmic x-axis. A baseline with an incomplete suite may appear in the scatterplots for its completed benchmarks, but it is excluded from cross-benchmark critical-difference analysis unless it has the full common benchmark panel.
* Produce uncertainty-aware normalized critical-difference diagrams with and without a FLOP control. Normalize scores within each benchmark across the complete-panel cohort. Estimate each score's task-level sample SEM from the scored trial rewards, then multiply the SEM by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` to account conservatively for the policy's 10% infrastructure-failure tolerance. With a fixed random seed, draw 100,000 score panels from independent normal sampling distributions centered on the reported scores and clipped to the metric's `[0, 1]` range. Rank models within every benchmark for each draw, using average ranks for ties, and report mean ranks with simultaneous 95% bands based on the draw-wise maximum absolute rank deviation. Report the Nemenyi critical difference at `alpha = 0.05`; it depends on the number of models and benchmarks, while score uncertainty affects the simulated rank distribution and its simultaneous bands.
* For the FLOP-controlled diagram, regress the draw's benchmark-normalized scores on `log10(total training FLOPs)` with one common linear slope, rank the within-benchmark residuals, and otherwise use the same uncertainty procedure. Treat FLOP estimates as fixed point estimates and disclose that their estimation uncertainty is not propagated. The uncontrolled diagram ranks the sampled normalized scores directly.
* We use a 6ND proxy for pretraining FLOPS, and 6 * max_tokens_per_rollout / max_context_length * n_rollouts * active_params proxy for RL FLOPS; that said, we are the only lab, as of this writing, which releases RL FLOPS, so meaningful comparisons are impossible. From the few labs who release midtraining / SFT information, we derive an unweighted mean percentage of FLOPS devoted to midtraining. We then estimate midtraining FLOPS for other labs using that mean. We estimate total FLOPS as the sum of pretraining FLOPS + (all midtraining / non-RL) FLOPS + (all RL and OPD) FLOPS. For any model which doesn't give sufficient evidence for any of the three stages, use the mean FLOPS over all models in the cohort as the estimated  FLOPS for that stage.
* In a separate standalone table, include all raw scores in XX.y format, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the trial count and the infrastructure error tolerance -- do not leave gaps, use table captions for results that require further context, use the exact same model family in the table as was present in the x-y scatterplot(s)
* Eval results are reportable IFF the eval in question completed with no more than 10% of trials encountering infrastructure errors
* Eval results are reportable IFF they include provenance, in the form of model traces, and where available, verifier traces
* Any eval result that is publicly presented should clearly distinguish whether the benchmarks are in-distribution (part of the dev set), held out, or a mix of the two
* Any eval result that is publicly presented in a major release should report on *all* ID and OOD benchmarks, avoiding cherry picking, substitution, or new evals outside of a formal policy update
* For active development and internal communication, it is fine to define working subsets of the ID benchmarks and report on those in isolation

## Future considerations

* We would like to post-train multiple Snowball checkpoints, experimenting with different degrees of compute applied to post-training, to establish trade-off lines / domains
* We would like to think about a "marin model card" that would set minimum standards for true open development
* amd/Instella-MoE-16B-A3B-Think is not runnable currently from our pinned vLLM fork, but we would like to look at this model in the future

* JudgeArena multilingual, maybe one of those cultural idiom / include benchmarks, restore simpleQA-mini, a long context supplement for MRCR
* Produce a summary of why we think the previously flagged TB2 / TB4 task description overlap are likely not problematic, if they are not
* Use stirrup for at least one eval
* Find a better instruction following benchmark than IFBench
* Consider a subset of MMLU-Pro and tau-bench so they run faster

topics.title: Add GB200 launcher and H100 pipeline validation
topics.body:
Add a GB200 pipeline launcher and a bounded H100 validation runner for the model recipe from main `89ac0d770506f7e27ca217760ec5ca3246694e7e`. The launcher uses FP32 parameters, BF16 compute, compute-scaled MuonH, SM100 ragged transport and Flash Attention. It requests one hard NVLink domain in the opportunistic BATCH queue and separates queue wait from worker execution deadlines. Future run names use `pipeline-gb200-*` or `pipeline-h100-*`.

Executable `0da04acccf7b0842319a8668d71ccc697a7b10ec` completed the corrected eight-GB200 gate with two full-width layers, PP2/EP4 and sequence length 4096. The two losses were 11.806337356567383 and 0.4912489652633667. All eight native GPU processes, both Iris GPU tasks and the coordinator exited zero. All 48 startup task ABI records had zero input memory-kind mismatches. Both coordinator failure and preemption retry caps were zero; the SDK launch example sets both explicitly because the CLI retry option controls failure retries only. [GB200 setup and standalone commands](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/experiments/grug/moe_hero_pipeline/GB200.md) record prerequisites and acceptance criteria.

The combined H100 runner was validated at `a1e3ab278eeb05bb645db641dd3e7dabedf90dbb` on 16 H100s with two full-width layers, PP2/EP8 and sequence length 4096. Ten synthetic updates had finite losses from 11.804966926574707 to 0.4793720245361328. Twenty fresh Harrier updates consumed 2,621,440 tokens with finite losses from 11.8075590133667 to 7.612007141113281. All 200 raw components remained nonempty with their original mixture weights and order. Both GPU tasks and supervisors exited zero; fresh-data logs retain 15 individual rank exits, while the supervisor's child-reaping contract certifies all 16. No checkpoint was written. These runs used the explicit SM90 pooled-wave/FA4 adapter with SYRK disabled and establish no H100 ragged-transport parity. [H100 reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/docs/references/hero-pipeline-h100.md) separates these runs from the historical reduced-model checkpoint comparison.

The runtime pins upstream JAXPP `328f75a80cecf22c7cc030a82d8941d3c1e220b6` plus a tracked host-memory/startup overlay. JAX 0.11.1 overrides JAXPP's declared compatibility cap and remains experimental; CUDA dependencies with lower bounds are recorded per launch. Installer recovery avoids duplicate global reinstall flags, including on deployed older worker wrappers. The [Iris installer incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/600) distinguishes the initiating GitHub fetch failure from the broken recovery command. Main-recipe argument parsing rejects AdamW before distributed initialization. Shared pipeline configuration, process ownership, array predicates, data scheduling and loader cleanup consolidate the overlapping work from #9279 and #9460.

Required lint, type checks, hooks and strict docs checks passed. The affected safe suite passed 5,562 tests with 18 skips and six expected failures. The lint-catalog review completed; findings were fixed or answered. Before merge, the positional compiled-initialization triple must be replaced with a named result and the runner lifecycle split further. Those deferred structural changes need separate transport and lifecycle validation.

Full 48-layer main-recipe execution remains unvalidated. The 64-GB200 rack attempt acquired its allocation and started some native processes, then failed during runtime installation; it produced no finite training updates. The full 192-H100/48-layer/65K run remains held. This pull request remains draft.

topics.title: Experiment: Hero throughput and expert drops at 8K and 16K context
topics.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

topics.title: [grug] Raise hero single-rack MFU from 28.2% to 31.1%
topics.body:
On one GB200 NVL72 rack, these commits shorten the `moe_hero_ep` training step from 13.90 to 12.61 s (28.24% to 31.13% MFU), with loss inside the run-to-run noise of unchanged code. The last commit adds a PGLE profile builder; with a profile built from the program's own trace, the step is 12.52 s (31.37% MFU). The changes come from two campaigns: the first worked down the step's most expensive scopes, and the second benchmarked OLMo-core 3's BF16 MoE kernels against this path (#9636) and kept the leads that paid.

Each row is one single-rack run (`cw-us-east-08a`, 64 GPUs) restored from `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k` step 180000, seed 0, 100 steps, on main's production PJRT wheel with the code's defaults. The time is the median step duration over steps 180011-180099 without the three profiled steps, and the gain is the previous row's time divided by this row's, minus one. Repeated runs of the same code differ by about 0.1%. The runs used trees from before a final round of refactors and review fixes (types, helpers, comments, tests, and code paths the hero does not take); the hero's train step lowers to the same program at these commits.

| Change | Commit | s/step | MFU | Gain |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main | b4d1761ff2 | 13.899 | 28.24% | |
| Remat discounts the host-offloaded carry | 13448300c6 | 13.737 | 28.57% | +1.18% |
| Unfilled ragged transport buffers | a544f2571c | 13.542 | 28.99% | +1.44% |
| Expert-side routing-weight gradient | 9ea5098c10 | 13.130 | 29.90% | +3.14% |
| Streaming Triton short convolution | 98412f4efc | 13.059 | 30.06% | +0.55% |
| SwiGLU backward in the dh GEMM epilogue | 50e50512a5 | 12.943 | 30.33% | +0.89% |
| Device-side kernel availability check | 1f08c52720 | | | no hero change |
| Triton router top-k | 42fc5766b3 | 12.875 | 30.49% | +0.53% |
| Token-major dispatch scatter | 0ba2cb6bbd | 12.730 | 30.83% | +1.14% |
| Shared and chunk GEMMs under the MoE transports | 45c2459f70 | 12.638 | 31.06% | +0.73% |
| Synchronous collectives without the carry offload | 8fd3af2759 | | | no hero change |
| Shared-expert SwiGLU in QuACK epilogues | ffecc63a46 | 12.652 | 31.03% | -0.11% |
| No routed pre-activation store under remat | 9ce3cfc1a4 | 12.611 | 31.13% | +0.33% |
| PGLE profile builder, run with a profile | daa46e2be5 | 12.515 | 31.37% | +0.77% |

The scheduling row groups three changes that do not stand alone. The MLP-section weight prefetch (from #9481) lets the first shared expert's gate/up projection run beside the first ragged dispatch, but it also moves a weight slice behind each layer's carry offload copy on the same memcpy stream, which stalls the forward for 98-152 ms/step on the production wheel. The barrier that issues the slices before the carry copy removes that stall, and costs 0.49% on a program that does not collide; at the end of the series, disabling it alone slows the step by 0.79%. The shared-expert QuACK row is negative because, after the scheduling row, the shared GEMMs are what covers the transports: the 0.18 s/step of compute it saves left 0.24 s/step more transport exposed. Removing it from the end of the series still slows the step, by 0.35% and 0.22% in two pairs, so it stays.

Changes whose gain was below about 0.3% were removed from the final tip one at a time and kept only if the tip slowed by more than 0.2% without them; a result between 0.2% and 0.4% got a second pair. That dropped a scatter-based inverse permutation (the tip was 0.04% faster without it) and a Triton bincount (0.22% and 0.10%), and kept the routed pre-activation change (0.47%) and the shared-expert QuACK change. The four rows from the unfilled transport buffers through the dh-epilogue SwiGLU backward were measured with the inverse permutation in their base and before a behavior-neutral review cleanup; without it, the last of them ran the same 12.943 s.

Numerics: the unfilled transport buffers, the top-k kernel, the dispatch scatter and the pre-activation change are bitwise. The routing-weight gradient, the dh-epilogue SwiGLU backward and the short convolution's weight gradient change at bf16 rounding; the shared-expert SwiGLU now runs on the fp32 accumulator, so the forward changes at rounding level and 0.06-0.3% of routing assignments differ downstream, as close to an fp32 reference as before; the carry barrier moves fusion boundaries. On the ragged backend, an accepted assignment whose combine weight is zero, or small enough for `w * dout` to underflow, gets a zero combine-weight gradient rather than `<dout, y>`, which `moe_mlp` documents; sigmoid and softmax routers produce such weights only by underflow, where their logit gradient is as small. Against main over 100 steps, the final tip's loss differs by at most 3.8e-4 (2.6e-4 with the profile), against 3.3e-4 between two runs of main. Four of about 30 runs took a late upward excursion of about 1e-3 that value-identical variants also showed, so it is run-to-run nondeterminism.

Peak HBM rises from 103.1 to 123.2 GiB of a 143.75 GiB pool, mainly the 18 GiB routed MoE output that the expert-side routing-weight gradient saves; under the carry offload the launcher defaults to `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.78` and slop 105, validated on one rack only. A ragged run without the carry offload keeps XLA's default scheduler, which ignores the one-in-flight collective limit, so that configuration now runs collectives synchronously; the hero always offloads and is unaffected. PGLE needs a profile built from a trace of the exact program and mesh, so the production run needs its own before it gains the last row; automatic PGLE stays off. The memcpy-stream collision is avoided per program here; the patched PJRT wheel that gives host transfers their own streams is left for a follow-up.

This supersedes #9481: it carries that PR's mirror transpose parameters, weight prefetch and PGLE builder, and replaces its two-stage chunk pipelining with the dispatch overlap above, which with PGLE measured 12.666 s/step against 12.783 for pipelining with PGLE, the latter on a patched PJRT wheel without the copy stall (both before the kernels above and the shared-expert change). Part of #9636; the OLMo-core comparison and its adopt/defer/reject table are on that issue. Research records: `.agents/logbooks/mfu30.md` and `.agents/logbooks/olmo9636.md` on `research/mcwitt/mfu30`.

topics.title: [eval] Check in the September evaluation campaign
topics.body:
Check in the model, evaluator, and launcher configurations for the September 2026 evaluation campaign, together with the runtime fixes needed for serving, retry, resume, and coverage. The launcher validates external pins, writes immutable effective-config snapshots, and accepts an optional submitter-controlled version label. That label does not attest policy conformance.

Harbor results are bound to the full model and hosted judge configurations, dataset, policy, runtime, and task limit. Resume checks this identity before submission and reuse. A changed checkpoint under the same served name is rejected, as are existing roots without model-bound provenance. Recovery retries known infrastructure failures and unscored trials while retaining scored outcomes and unknown errors.

The frozen Harbor runtime pins 94b118022fe3e677784a638daf33d57a836fa5fe and includes the Tau3 adapter. The Evalchemy lock and generated pin match Marin's external dependency configuration.

SWE-bench uses the native Mini-SWE adapter from merged [Harbor #232](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/232) and [#233](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/233). Its 32,768-token context includes the prompt and reply together. Mini-SWE counts the rendered prompt through the serving tokenizer, including tools and the generation prefix, and caps the reply within the remaining budget and server window. Harbor loads Mini-SWE's base configuration before applying overrides and selects its batch agent, which saves the trajectory on context exhaustion without prompting. Harbor can then verify the existing patch.

Sotopia uses the packaged agent from merged [Harbor #231](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/231). Judge failures become verifier infrastructure errors. The Marin agent wrappers and their harness dependencies are removed. Sotopia's native generation still does not enforce its declared context budget, so those results cannot establish conformance to the 32K context policy.

Part of #9566.

topics.title: [eval] Qwen3.6 tau3 context and output-length ablation
topics.body:
## TL;DR

With Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on Harbor τ³-bench through Pi ACP, the 131,072-token total context / 32,768-token per-turn output arm had the highest observed scoreable-trial reward: 153/373 = 0.410. It is the selected campaign setting. The comparison is model-specific and does not prove that 131k is a universal context saturation point.

## Description

The current campaign's historical 32k/8k run scored 0.068, versus 0.252 in an earlier campaign at 73,728/8,192. Those runs used different Harbor revisions and are not a controlled context comparison. The diagnostic grid used the same pinned Qwen3.6 revision and the Harbor τ³ benchmark with Pi ACP. Each full arm contains 375 trials. “Score” below divides wins by *scoreable* trials; Harbor's displayed aggregate mean also counts completed but unscored attempts as zero, so its denominator is different.

| Total context / per-turn output | Wins / scoreable trials | Scoreable-only estimate | Status | Archive |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| 65,536 / 16,384 | 75/372 | 0.202 | Sealed | [results](s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261004-001237-Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-tau3-65k-16k-tau3-65k-16k-f0e0/results) |
| 65,536 / 32,768 | 52/218 | 0.239 | Partial estimate, **not sealed**; below 90% coverage | [results](s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261004-090453-Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-tau3-65k-32k-tau3-65k-32k-5e2a/results) |
| 131,072 / 32,768 | 153/373 | 0.410 | Sealed; selected | [results](s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261004-001235-Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-tau3-131k-32k-tau3-131k-32k-a80a/results) |
| 131,072 / 65,536 | 118/355 | 0.332 | Early sealed at 94.7% coverage | [results](s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261004-113601-Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-tau3-131k-65k-tau3-131k-65k-ca48/results) |
| 262,144 / 65,536 | 144/373 | 0.386 | Early sealed at 99.5% coverage | [results](s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261004-113801-Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-tau3-262k-65k-tau3-262k-65k-43da/results) |

The 65k/32k arm was stopped with 47 τ³ runtime infrastructure failures, chiefly repeated user-model service unavailability; its 0.239 is an incomplete estimate, not a policy-valid result. The 131k/65k and 262k/65k roots were stopped after passing the campaign's 90% scoreable-coverage threshold. At a fixed 65k output cap, 262k context outscored 131k context, so longer context may still help. At 131k context, raising the per-turn cap from 32k to 65k did not improve the observed score.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Identify a τ³ context/output setting that recovers the historical Qwen3.6 performance under a controlled current harness before re-running the model panel.

## Status

Complete. The canonical τ³ config uses Pi `max_input_tokens=131072` and `max_output_tokens=32768`, with τ³-only serving overrides at `max_model_len=131072` where the pinned model supports it. Two pinned models whose native context is 32,768 remain at that native limit. The implementation is [Marin commit 929edc7cc8](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/929edc7cc8cce19347f8b3669f1022d3025afdc3). Configs and trial archives are retained in the campaign artifacts. These runs are diagnostic and carry no released-policy attestation.

## Links

- [Canonical τ³ config and serving overrides](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/929edc7cc8cce19347f8b3669f1022d3025afdc3/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled)
- [Earlier public context-length ablation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10420)

## Decision Log

- Select 131k/32k for the panel re-run because it is the best score among these scoreable arms and avoids the extra serving cost of 262k/65k.
- Retain the 65k/32k estimate with its denominator and infrastructure caveat; do not seal it.
- Re-run every τ³ tracker cell under the new canonical config rather than transferring Qwen3.6's effect to other models by assumption.

## Conclusion

The tested 131k/32k arm recovered Qwen3.6 τ³ reward to 0.410 (153/373) under the current diagnostic setup. Panel-wide benefit and context saturation remain unproven until the re-runs finish.

topics.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
topics.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. topics.title: [canary-grug-multislice] JAX startup stalls after unequal task retries
topics.body:
The October 4 two-slice Grug smoke timed out after 135 minutes. Worker failures caused independent task retries, and the child did not complete JAX distributed startup. This recurs from #9723; #8940 tracks the coordinator naming bug, and #8941 is the open fix.

Reproduce:
1. Submit `python -m experiments.ferries.grug_multislice_smoke` through Iris with two `v6e-8` slices.
2. Let one task retry independently during JAX startup, as happened here after worker failures. Compare the `initialize_jax bootstrap inputs` logs for both tasks.

Expected: both tasks resolve one coordinator despite unequal retry numbers, then complete the five training steps.

In Finelog `marin` / `log`, task 0 attempt 2 (`0:2`) and task 1 attempt 1 (`1:1`) both entered JAX initialization at 16:38:57 UTC. They used `jax_coordinator-attempt-2` and `jax_coordinator-attempt-1`, respectively. [The Iris initializer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6940dbb764856c9b286eac3b800e3fa36b0753a0/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/init.py#L279) appends each task's own attempt number to this shared endpoint name. Attempt `1:1` later exited 139 after `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` on `CoordinationService/RegisterTask` at 17:09:02 UTC. Iris had requeued both logical tasks by 17:48 UTC; the Actions wait step had expired at 17:43:34 UTC.

topics.title: [rl] Snowball broad-domain RLVR across cooldown variants
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Broad-domain RLVR on Snowball 67B A2B variants produced short-run gains and repeated training instability. The six-arm Datakit loop/length sweep showed fewer length stops with a length penalty, without a clear holdout accuracy gain. A three-arm turn-budget sweep reduced first-batch temperature-1 length stops to 9.7% at 48K tokens per turn, versus 12.7% at 32K and 18.4% at 16K. The unpenalized Antidoom run peaked at 34/100 holdout pass@1 at step 12, then reached 2/100 at step 20; its step-12 policy is public. Starting from that policy, the reference/KL arm reached its best completed evaluation on the same 100-prompt holdout at step 20: 42/100 pass@1 and 0.4465 normalized average verifier score. The reference/KL checkpoint was selected using this holdout repeatedly, so 42/100 is a selection result rather than an independent test score. The Antidoom v2 and reference/KL results should not be treated as a matched cross-run comparison.

## Description

The September 21 [Datakit SFT checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21) and its [September 23 GLM53 SFT continuation](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-GLM53-RLVR-SFT-2026.09.23) seeded the first lineages. Later arms started from an Antidoom FTPO/DAPO step-45 policy export. Its tokenizer and chat-template hashes matched the September 21 model; the archived record does not establish exact weight ancestry. The later Datakit and Antidoom full-size recipes sampled math, coding, instruction following, tool use, and other Nemotron Ultra RLVR environments. Their standard layout used 80 H100 policy GPUs and 48 H100 inference GPUs, 512 prompts × 16 samples per optimizer step, Megatron router replay, and evaluations on about 100 holdout prompts. Earlier GLM53 jobs and smoke trials had different layouts. The launch configs record variations in reward shaping, context limits, loss reduction, reference/KL, and runtime fixes.

The [public campaign archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-broad-domain-rlvr-campaign-2026) contains the Marin launcher and configs, per-run reward and timing figures, metric tables, verifier audits, and the turn-budget results. It excludes original training datasets and raw response archives. The [canonical config gist](https://gist.github.com/penfever/1eb3aa510ce7870bb22e7bef10b8d940) covers the main lineages; the [penalty sweep gist](https://gist.github.com/penfever/c57d976ed11a7f63c682884e4628c0ca) and [turn-budget gist](https://gist.github.com/penfever/e05a6e78953d06861d2a32e9b4b99644) preserve the other experimental configs.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Determine whether broad-domain verifier rewards can improve a Snowball policy while keeping answer completion and exploration stable. Test loop/length shaping, longer generation budgets, entropy loss, policy-loss reduction, and a frozen reference with KL after the unpenalized run collapsed.

## Status

The campaign runs are complete or stopped. The table links each locally named run family to its public archive; smoke trials and retries are documented inside those run records.

| [GLM53 RLVR1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-broad-domain-rlvr-campaign-2026/tree/main/runs/glm53-rlvr1) | September 23 GLM53 RLVR SFT | Stopped after step 71; early baseline for reward and timing. Per-domain history was not recoverable. |

- September 29–30: Completed the loop/length penalty sweep; selected loop 2 / length 0.1 as a compromise for a longer run despite the sweep's inconclusive accuracy ranking.
- September 30–October 1: Tested 16K, 32K, and 48K turn caps. Selected 48K to reduce training length stops, then tried a larger total window.
- October 2–3: Switched to the Antidoom step-45 policy without loop/length penalties. Preserved the v2 step-12 peak before its collapse. Tried entropy/sequence-mean and token-mean continuations.
- October 3–4: Added a frozen reference and KL loss, corrected memory and credential faults, resumed from a protected step-4 checkpoint, and selected the step-20 peak by completed holdout pass@1 with average score as tie-breaker. The KL arm counts its optimizer steps from zero at the v2 step-12 starting weights; its resume checkpoint was step 4 of the KL arm.

## Conclusion

The campaign established runnable 128-GPU broad-domain RLVR recipes, verifier diagnostics, and durable model snapshots. In the six-arm sweep, length penalties reduced final holdout length stops in each matched pair (48% to 15%, 22% to 6%, and 52% to 23%). In the separate turn-budget sweep, the first temperature-1 training batch had fewer length stops at longer caps. Neither experiment established a general accuracy gain. The reference/KL arm's selected step-20 holdout was 42/100 versus 35/100 at its resumed step 4 under the same configured validation set; subsequent steps 22–30 ranged from 33/100 to 37/100. The small, repeatedly used holdout does not establish external generalization. Several arms degraded sharply, and the available runs do not isolate one cause for those failures. The configs, raw numeric metrics, and selected figures remain available for a larger matched evaluation.

topics.title: Support context-length switches in the hero run
topics.body:
Let the hero switch context length mid-run without changing its training schedule. The ladder launcher takes `--seq-len` and holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, gate/router weight decay, and `run_progress` therefore match the 4K run. A changed context requires an explicit `--qk-mult`, applied to all attention layers; `--capacity-factor` overrides the expert receiver capacity.

Harrier now shuffles blocks of 2^20 tokens (`io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len`), which equals the existing 256-sequence block at 4K. At a longer context the outer block permutation stays the same, so only each cell's in-progress 512-block window reorders. With the previous sequence-sized blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T. At 16K the past main-mixture boundary moves from step 108000 to 108096, and a continuation must pass `--accept-mixture-boundary-shift`.

Canonical hero eval stays at 4K packing, so the inherited `eval_dropless/*` series remains comparable, and the first-step eval now also runs after a checkpoint resume. Per-example FLOPs rise with context, so a FLOPs baseline (`--flops-baseline-step`, `--flops-baseline-total`) keeps `throughput/total_gflops` continuous across the handoff. `trigger_hero.sh` records the context, QK multiplier, capacity, eval context, FLOPs baseline, and boundary acceptance in the W&B lineage and the #8506 launch record. `launch_diagnostics` gains `--optimizer-tokens-per-step`, `--gate-router-weight-decay`, `--eval-seq-len`, and `--eval-prefix`, so a one-rack rehearsal can use the hero's optimizer settings and report long-context eval separately.

The live run is unchanged. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

topics.title: [canary-grug-multislice] JAX startup hangs after task 0 retry
topics.body:
The October 3 Grug multislice canary timed out after 135 minutes with its Iris training child still running. JAX startup could not complete after the two tasks reached different retry numbers. No training step was observed.

Reproduce:
1. Start a two-task Iris JAX job and let task 0 retry while task 1 remains on its first attempt.
2. Run `initialize_jax` on both tasks. Task 0 publishes `jax_coordinator-attempt-1`; task 1 polls `jax_coordinator-attempt-0`.

Expected: both tasks resolve the same coordinator after an independent task retry.

Finelog `marin` / `log` for this child shows task `0:1` advertising `jax_coordinator-attempt-1` at 16:35:52 UTC and task `1:0` polling `jax_coordinator-attempt-0` at 16:35:58. At 17:05:57, JAX aborted task 0 with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` on `CoordinationService/RegisterTask` (exit 139); task 1 then raised `TimeoutError` after 1800 seconds waiting for the attempt-0 endpoint. Iris records task `0:0` as `worker_failed` before the divergent retries. The Actions wait step expired at 17:03:59, before those terminal errors.

[The Iris initializer appends each task's own attempt ID](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/init.py#L278-L279), then task 0 registers that name and task 1 resolves it. [#8940](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8940) already identifies independent attempt IDs as unsafe for shared coordinator names; [#8941](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8941) is open. This canary is a concrete recurrence while that fix is pending.

<summary>Durable log keys</summary>

- `/runner/iris-run-job-20261003-144844/grug-train-grug-multislice-smoke-37130915330-1/0:1`

**Why:** in batch 178, moving routed work onto the shared expert did nothing at 2817 steps, or cost loss once it was strong enough to change behavior. The capacity argument says the routed experts only run short of room when overtrained, so this tests the two most informative forms at 100× the tokens.

- **Reads:** final Paloma vs `ot100-base` (the launcher only evaluates at the end); training loss, routed share, cos(s, r) and shadow R² over training. Does the compressible share of the routed output, or the gap between arms, move as the run goes on?
- **Timing:** ~4.7 steps/s, ~17 h each.

| step | base | xfer04 | gap16 |

| 60k | 1.730 | 1.735 | 1.742 |
| 135k | 1.642 | 1.644 | 1.653 |

The transfer term rewards scaling `s` along `r`, and AttnRes normalizes each source, so extra scale costs the LM nothing. The logs only hold ratios, so absolute ‖s‖ / ‖r‖ are needed to tell.
- **Ops:** `ot100-base` hit a NaN loss at step 49,041. It resumed from the step-44,932 checkpoint and replayed the same data cleanly, so the NaN looks like a one-off flake, not a reproducible instability.

> Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):
>
> 1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
> 2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.

> 4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.
>
> Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:
>

> 2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.
>
> These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.
